# 82nd Golden Globe Awards – Television Winners

The **82nd Golden Globe Awards** ceremony took place on January 5, 2025, at The Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills. Hosted by comedian Nikki Glaser (the first solo female host in the show's history), the event honored American television productions of 2024.

## Television Category Winners

### Best Television Series – Drama
- **Shōgun** (FX / Hulu) — *Shōgun (2024 TV series)*

### Best Television Series – Musical or Comedy
- **Hacks** (Max)

### Best Limited Series, Anthology Series, or Motion Picture Made for Television
- **Baby Reindeer** (Netflix)
- **The Diplomat** (Netflix)
- **Disclaimer** (Apple TV+)
- **Hacks** (Max)
- **Monsters: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story** (Netflix)
- **Mr. & Mrs. Smith** (Amazon Prime Video)
- **Nobody Wants This** (Netflix)
- **The Penguin** (HBO / Max)
- **Ripley** (Netflix)
- **True Detective: Night Country** (HBO / Max)

### Best Performance in Stand-Up Comedy on Television
- **Ali Wong** – *Ali Wong: Single Lady* (Netflix)  
  *(Nikki Glaser was nominated but lost to Ali Wong)*

### Best Actor in a Television Series – Drama
- **Hiroyuki Sanada** – *Shōgun* (FX / Hulu) as Lord Yoshii Toranaga

### Best Actress in a Television Series – Drama
- **Anna Sawai** – *Shōgun* (FX / Hulu) as Toda Mariko

### Best Actor in a Television Series – Musical or Comedy
- **Jeremy Allen White** – *The Bear* (FX / Hulu) as Carmen "Carmy" Berzatto

### Best Actress in a Television Series – Musical or Comedy
- **Jean Smart** – *Hacks* (Max) as Deborah Vance

### Best Actor in a Limited Series, Anthology Series, or Motion Picture Made for Television
- **Colin Farrell** – *The Penguin* (HBO / Max) as Oswald "Oz" Cobb / The Penguin

### Best Actress in a Limited Series, Anthology Series, or Motion Picture Made for Television
- **Jodie Foster** – *True Detective: Night Country* (HBO / Max) as Chief Liz Danvers

### Best Supporting Actor on Television
- **Tadanobu Asano** – *Shōgun* (FX / Hulu) as Kashigi Yabushige

### Best Supporting Actress on Television
- **Jessica Gunning** – *Baby Reindeer* (Netflix) as Martha Scott

---

## Notable Highlights
- **Emilia Pérez** (film) won most nominations overall with 10, but its film wins were separate from these TV results.
- **Shōgun** dominated television, winning four awards including Best Television Series – Drama.
- **Hacks** secured two major wins, including Best Television Series – Musical or Comedy.
- **The Bear** led TV nominations with five entries, making it the most-nominated series that year.
- **Viola Davis** received the Cecil B. DeMille Award during the untelevised gala dinner prior to the main ceremony.

The **82nd Golden Globe Awards** was an awards ceremony that honored [excellence in film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_film "2024 in film") and [American television productions of 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_American_television "2024 in American television"). The winners were revealed during the live telecast, airing on [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") and streaming on [Paramount+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount+ "Paramount+") on January 5, 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-2) The event was hosted by comedian [Nikki Glaser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikki_Glaser "Nikki Glaser"), making her the first solo female host in Golden Globes history.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Glaser-3)

The nominations were announced live on December 9, 2024, at a [press conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press_conference "Press conference") at [the Beverly Hilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beverly_Hilton "The Beverly Hilton") by actors [Morris Chestnut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Chestnut "Morris Chestnut") and [Mindy Kaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindy_Kaling "Mindy Kaling"), following an introduction from Golden Globes president, Helen Hoenhe.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Globes-4) *[Emilia Pérez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilia_Pérez "Emilia Pérez")*, with 10 nominations, became the most nominated comedy/musical film in [Golden Globes history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Awards#Superlatives "Golden Globe Awards"), just 1 shy of the overall record of 11, set by [Robert Altman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman "Robert Altman")'s [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") [satire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire_(film_and_television) "Satire (film and television)") *[Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville_(film) "Nashville (film)")* in the drama category in [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Golden_Globe_Awards "33rd Golden Globe Awards").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-5) *[The Brutalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Brutalist "The Brutalist")* received the second-most in film with 7 nominations, followed by *[Conclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conclave_(film) "Conclave (film)")* with 6.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-6) Additionally, *[The Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bear_(TV_series) "The Bear (TV series)")* led the television nominations with 5, followed by *[Only Murders in the Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Only_Murders_in_the_Building "Only Murders in the Building")* and *[Shōgun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shōgun_(2024_TV_series) "Shōgun (2024 TV series)")* with 4 each.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Variety-7)

## Ceremony information

On August 28, 2024, comedian [Nikki Glaser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikki_Glaser "Nikki Glaser") was announced as the host for this year's ceremony, following last year's widely criticized host, comedian [Jo Koy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Koy "Jo Koy").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Glaser-3) She is the first woman to host the Golden Globes solo.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-8) Glaser herself was nominated for [Best Performance in Stand-Up Comedy on Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Performance_in_Stand-Up_Comedy_on_Television "Golden Globe Award for Best Performance in Stand-Up Comedy on Television") for her [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") comedy special, *Nikki Glaser: Someday You'll Die*,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Governors-9) but lost to [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix")'s *Ali Wong: Single Lady*.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-10)

The ceremony was held at 5:00 p.m. [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone") / 8:00 p.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on January 5, 2025. It was broadcast live on [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") and streamed on [Paramount+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount+ "Paramount+").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Globes-4) [Glenn Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Weiss "Glenn Weiss") and [Ricky Kirshner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Kirshner "Ricky Kirshner") of White Cherry Entertainment returned from last year to executive produce the ceremony, along with [Dick Clark Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Clark_Productions "Dick Clark Productions").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Globes-4)

On December 3, 2024, it was announced that the two Lifetime Achievement Awards, which were not presented last year, would return this year; however, they were presented during an untelevised gala dinner on January 3, 2025, prior to the telecast, similar to the [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards")' [Governors Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governors_Awards "Governors Awards").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Governors-9) The recipient of the [Cecil B. DeMille Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Cecil_B._DeMille_Award "Golden Globe Cecil B. DeMille Award") was [Viola Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_Davis "Viola Davis"), while the [Carol Burnett Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Carol_Burnett_Award "Golden Globe Carol Burnett Award") was awarded to [Ted Danson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Danson "Ted Danson").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-11)

Aside from "El Mal", they were also jointly nominated for composing *Emilia Pérez*'s [Best Original Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Original_Score "Golden Globe Award for Best Original Score") and an additional Best Original Song nominee: "[Mi camino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mi_camino "Mi camino")".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Variety-7)

# *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*

Annual publication of university rankings

**Times Higher Education World University Rankings**

| [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/74/WUR_logo_large.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WUR_logo_large.jpg) | |
| --- | --- |
| Editor | Phil Baty |
| Categories | [Higher education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education "Higher education") |
| Frequency | Annual |
| Publisher | *[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education")* |
| First issue | 2004; 22 years ago (2004) (in partnership with *[QS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds")*)   2010; 16 years ago (2010) (on its own) |
| Country | [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") |
| Language | [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") & [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language") |
| Website | [www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/) |

The ***Times Higher Education World University Rankings***, often referred to as the **THE Rankings**, is the annual publication of [university rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_ranking "University ranking") by the *[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education")* magazine. The publisher had collaborated with [Quacquarelli Symonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds") (QS) to publish the joint *[THE-QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education–QS_World_University_Rankings "Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings")* from 2004 to 2009 before it turned to [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters") for a new ranking system from 2010 to 2013. In 2014, the magazine signed an agreement with [Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier") to provide it with the data used in compiling its annual rankings.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-1)

The publication includes global rankings of universities, including by subject and reputation. It also has begun publishing three regional tables for universities in [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia"), [Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America"), and [BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS") and emerging economies, which are ranked with separate criteria and weightings.

The THE Rankings is often considered one of the most widely observed university rankings together with the *[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_Ranking_of_World_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")* and the *[QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QS_World_University_Rankings "QS World University Rankings")*.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-:0-4) It is praised for having a new, improved ranking methodology since 2010, but criticism and concerns have been voiced that this methodology underestimates [non-science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-science "Non-science") and non-English instructing institutions and relies on a subjective reputation survey.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-:0-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise1-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-6)

## History

The creation of the original *[Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education–QS_World_University_Rankings "Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings")* has been attributed to [John O'Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_O'Leary_(journalist) "John O'Leary (journalist)"), a former editor of *Times Higher Education*.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-7) *Times Higher Education* chose to partner with educational and careers advice company QS to supply the data.

After the 2009 rankings, *Times Higher Education* took the decision to break from QS and signed an agreement with Thomson Reuters to provide the data for its annual World University Rankings from 2010 onwards. The publication developed a new rankings methodology in consultation with its readers, its editorial board and Thomson Reuters. Thomson Reuters will collect and analyse the data used to produce the rankings on behalf of Times Higher Education. The first ranking was published in September 2010.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-8)

Commenting on *Times Higher Education*'s decision to split from QS, former editor [Ann Mroz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Mroz "Ann Mroz") said, "universities deserve a rigorous, robust and transparent set of rankings – a serious tool for the sector, not just an annual curiosity." She went on to explain the reason behind the decision to continue to produce rankings without QS' involvement, saying that: "The responsibility weighs heavy on our shoulders...we feel we have a duty to improve how we compile them."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-9)

Phil Baty, editor of the new *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*, admitted in *[Inside Higher Ed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inside_Higher_Ed "Inside Higher Ed")*, "The rankings of the world's top universities that my magazine has been publishing for the past six years, and which have attracted enormous global attention, are not good enough. In fact, the surveys of reputation, which made up 40 percent of scores and which Times Higher Education until recently defended, had serious weaknesses. And it's clear that our research measures favored the sciences over the humanities."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-10)

He went on to describe previous attempts at peer review as "embarrassing" in *[The Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Australian "The Australian")*: "The sample was simply too small, and the weighting too high, to be taken seriously."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-11) THE published its first rankings using its new methodology on 16 September 2010, a month earlier than previous years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-timeshighereducation1-12)

In 2010, *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*, along with the QS World University Rankings and the *[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_Ranking_of_World_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")*, were described to be the three most influential international university rankings.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-edmont-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-15) *[The Globe and Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Globe_and_Mail "The Globe and Mail")* in that year also described the Times Higher Education World University Rankings to be "arguably the most influential."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-16)

In 2014 *Times Higher Education* announced a series of important changes to its flagship THE World University Rankings and its suite of global university performance analyses, following a strategic review by THE parent company TES Global.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-announces-reforms-17)

## Methodology

### Criteria and weighting

The inaugural 2010–2011 [methodology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodology "Methodology") contained 13 separate indicators grouped under five categories: Teaching (30 per cent of final score), research (30 per cent), citations (research impact) (worth 32.5 per cent), international mix (5 per cent), industry income (2.5 per cent). The number of indicators is up from the Times-QS rankings published between 2004 and 2009, which used six indicators.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

A draft of the inaugural methodology was released on 3 June 2010. The draft stated that 13 indicators would first be used and that this could rise to 16 in future rankings, and laid out the categories of indicators as "research indicators" (55 per cent), "institutional indicators" (25 per cent), "economic activity/innovation" (10 per cent), and "international diversity" (10 per cent).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-19) The names of the categories and the weighting of each was modified in the final methodology, released on 16 September 2010[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The final methodology also included the weighting assigned to each of the 13 indicators, shown below[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) (with some updates from 2022 to 2023 released methodology[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-20)):

| Overall indicator | Individual indicator | Percentage weighting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Industry Income – innovation | Research income from industry (per academic staff) | 2.5% |
| International diversity (currently: International outlook (staff, students, research)) | Ratio of international to domestic staffRatio of international to domestic studentsInternational Collaboration (as for 2022–23) | 3% (2.5% as for 2022–23)2% (2.5% as for 2022–23)2.5% (as for 2022–23) |
| Teaching – the learning environment | Reputational survey (teaching)PhDs awards per academicUndergrad. admitted per academicIncome per academicPhDs/undergraduate degrees awarded | 15%6%4.5%2.25%2.25% |
| Research – volume, income and reputation | Reputational survey (research)Research income (scaled)Papers per research and academic staffPublic research income/ total research income (currently cancelled) | 19.5% (18% as for 2022–23)5.25% (6% as for 2022–23)4.5% (6% as for 2022–23)/(currently cancelled, previously weighted 0.75%) |
| Citations – research influence | Citation impact (normalised average citation per paper) | 32.5% (30% as for 2022–23) |

The *Times Higher Education* billed the methodology as "robust, transparent and sophisticated", stating that the final methodology was selected after considering 10 months of "detailed consultation with leading experts in global higher education", 250 pages of feedback from "50 senior figures across every continent" and 300 postings on its website.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The overall ranking score was calculated by making [Z-scores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score "Standard score") all datasets to standardize different data types on a common scale to better make comparisons among data.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

The reputational component of the rankings (34.5 per cent of the overall score – 15 per cent for teaching and 19.5 per cent for research) came from an Academic Reputation Survey conducted by [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters") in spring 2010. The survey gathered 13,388 responses among scholars who, according to THE, were "statistically representative of global higher education's geographical and subject mix."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) However, the response rate of the survey in 2022-2024 was a mere 1.8%.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-22) The magazine's category for "industry income – innovation" came from a sole indicator, institution's research income from industry scaled against the number of academic staff." The magazine stated that it used this data as "proxy for high-quality knowledge transfer" and planned to add more indicators for the category in future years.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

Data for [citation impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_impact "Citation impact") (measured as a normalized average citation per paper), comprising 32.5 per cent of the overall score, came from 12,000 [academic journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal "Academic journal") [indexed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_index "Citation index") by Thomson Reuters' [Web of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_of_Science "Web of Science") database over the five years from 2004 to 2008. The *Times* stated that articles published in 2009–2010 have not yet completely accumulated in the database.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The normalization of the data differed from the previous rankings system and is intended to "reflect variations in citation volume between different subject areas," so that institutions with high levels of research activity in the [life sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_science "Life science") and other areas with high citation counts will not have an unfair advantage over institutions with high levels of research activity in the [social sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science"), which tend to use fewer citations on average.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

The magazine announced on 5 September 2011 that its 2011–2012 World University Rankings would be published on 6 October 2011.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Launch_Date-23) At the same time, the magazine revealed changes to the ranking formula that will be introduced with the new rankings. The methodology will continue to use 13 indicators across five broad categories and will keep its "fundamental foundations," but with some changes. Teaching and research will each remain 30 per cent of the overall score, and industry income will remain at 2.5 per cent. However, a new "international outlook – staff, students and research" will be introduced and will make up 7.5 per cent of the final score. This category will include the proportion of international staff and students at each institution (included in the 2011–2012 ranking under the category of "international diversity"), but will also add the proportion of research papers published by each institution that are co-authored with at least one international partner. One 2011–2012 indicator, the institution's public research income, will be dropped.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Launch_Date-23)

On 13 September 2011, the *Times Higher Education* announced that its 2011–2012 list will only rank the top 200 institutions. Phil Baty wrote that this was in the "interests of fairness," because "the lower down the tables you go, the more the data bunch up and the less meaningful the differentials between institutions become." However, Baty wrote that the rankings would include 200 institutions that fall immediately outside the official top 200 according to its data and methodology, but this "best of the rest" list from 201 to 400 would be unranked and listed alphabetically. Baty wrote that the magazine intentionally only ranks around 1 per cent of the world's universities in a recognition that "not every university should aspire to be one of the global research elite."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-24) However, the 2015/16 edition of the Times Higher Education World University Rankings ranks 800 universities, while Phil Baty announced that the 2016/17 edition, to be released on 21 September 2016, will rank "980 universities from 79 countries".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-26)

The methodology of the rankings was changed during the 2011–12 rankings process, with details of the changed methodology here.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-27) Phil Baty, the rankings editor, has said that the THE World University Rankings are the only global university rankings to examine a university's teaching environment, as others focus purely on research.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-28) Baty has also written that the THE World University Rankings are the only rankings to put arts and humanities and social sciences research on an equal footing to the sciences.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-29) However, this claim is no longer true. In 2015, QS introduced faculty area normalization to their QS World University Rankings, ensuring that citations data was weighted in a way that prevented universities specializing in the Life Sciences and Engineering from receiving undue advantage.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-30)

In November 2014, the magazine announced further reforms to the methodology after a review by parent company TES Global. The major change being all institutional data collection would be bought in house severing the connection with [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters"). In addition, research publication data would now be sourced from [Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier")'s [Scopus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopus "Scopus") database.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-announces-reforms-17)

### Reception

The reception to the methodology was varied.

Ross Williams of the [Melbourne Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Institute "Melbourne Institute"), commenting on the 2010–2011 draft, stated that the proposed methodology would favour more focused "science-based institutions with relatively few undergraduates" at the expense of institutions with more comprehensive programmes and undergraduates, but also stated that the indicators were "academically robust" overall and that the use of scaled measures would reward productivity rather than overall influence.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise1-5) [Steve Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Smith_(academic) "Steve Smith (academic)"), president of [Universities UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_UK "Universities UK"), praised the new methodology as being "less heavily weighted towards subjective assessments of reputation and uses more robust citation measures," which "bolsters confidence in the evaluation method."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise2-31) [David Willetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Willetts "David Willetts"), British [Minister of State for Universities and Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Business,_Innovation_and_Skills "Department for Business, Innovation and Skills") praised the rankings, noting that "reputation counts for less this time, and the weight accorded to quality in teaching and learning is greater."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise3-32) In 2014, David Willetts became chair of the TES Global Advisory Board, responsible for providing strategic advice to Times Higher Education.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-33)

### Criticism

Times Higher Education places a high importance on citations to generate rankings. Citations as a metric for effective education is problematic in many ways, placing universities who do not use English as their primary language at a disadvantage.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-34) Because English has been adopted as the international language for most academic societies and journals, citations and publications in a language different from English are harder to come across.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-35) Thus, such a methodology is criticized for being inappropriate and not comprehensive enough.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-RankingWatch-36) A second important disadvantage for universities of non-English tradition is that within the disciplines of social sciences and humanities the main tool for publications are books which are not or only rarely covered by digital citations records.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-37) In addition to these criticisms, the indicators used in the rankings have come under scrutiny. Several scholars, for example, have highlighted biases against [universities in the Arab region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education_in_the_Arab_world "Higher education in the Arab world") within existing rankings. They have advocated for the development of new methodologies that account for institutional disparities and ensure fair representation.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-39)

[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education") has also been criticized for its strong bias towards institutions that taught 'hard science' and had high quality output of research in these fields, often to the disadvantage of institutions focused on other subjects like the social sciences and humanities. For instance in the former [THE-QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THE-QS_World_University_Rankings "THE-QS World University Rankings"), the [London School of Economics (LSE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_London_School_of_Economics_and_Political_Science "The London School of Economics and Political Science") was ranked 11th in the world in 2004 and 2005, but dropped to 66th and 67th in the 2008 and 2009 edition.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-40) In January 2010, THE concluded the method employed by [Quacquarelli Symonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds"), who conducted the survey on their behalf, was flawed in such a way that bias was introduced against certain institutions, including LSE.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-autogenerated4-41)

A representative of [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters"), THE's new partner, commented on the controversy: "*LSE stood at only 67th in the last Times Higher Education-QS World University Rankings – some mistake surely? Yes, and quite a big one*."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-autogenerated4-41) Nonetheless, after the change of data provider to Thomson Reuters the following year, LSE fell to 86th place, with the ranking described by a representative of Thomson Reuters as 'a fair reflection of their status as a world class university'.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-lse.ac.uk-42) [LSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") despite being ranked continuously near the top in its national rankings, has been placed below other British universities in the Times Higher Education World Rankings in recent years, other institutions such as [Sciences Po](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sciences_Po "Sciences Po") have suffered due to the inherent methodology bias still used.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] [Trinity College Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College_Dublin "Trinity College Dublin")'s ranking in 2015 and 2016 was lowered by a basic mistake in data it had submitted; education administrator [Bahram Bekhradnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahram_Bekhradnia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bahram Bekhradnia (page does not exist)") said the fact this went unnoticed evinced a "very limited checking of data" "on the part of those who carry out such rankings". Bekhradnia also opined "while Trinity College was a respected university which could be relied upon to provide honest data, unfortunately that was not the case with all universities worldwide."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-43)

In general it is not clear who the rankings are made for. Many students, especially the undergraduate students, are not interested in the scientific work of a facility of higher education. Also the price of the education has no effects on the ranking. That means that private universities on the North American continent are compared to the European universities. Many European countries like France, Sweden or Germany for example have a long tradition on offering free education within facilities of higher education.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-45)

In 2021, the [University of Tsukuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tsukuba "University of Tsukuba") in [Ibaraki Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibaraki_Prefecture "Ibaraki Prefecture"), Japan, was alleged to have submitted falsified data on the number of international students enrolled at the university to the Times Higher Education World University Rankings.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-universityworldnews.com-46) The discovery resulted in an investigation by THE and the provision of guidance to the university on the submission of data,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-universityworldnews.com-46) however, it also led to the criticism amongst faculty members of the ease with which THE's ranking system could be abused. The matter was discussed in Japan's National Diet on April 21, 2021.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-47)

Seven Indian Institutes of Technology (Mumbai, Delhi, Kanpur, Guwahati, Madras, Roorkee and Kharagpur) have boycotted THE rankings from 2020. These IITs have not participated in the rankings citing concerns over transparency.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-48) [Sorbonne University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorbonne_University "Sorbonne University")'s President [Nathalie Drach-Temam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathalie_Drach-Temam "Nathalie Drach-Temam") announced in October 2025 that they would no longer participate in the Times Higher Education rankings. [Zurich University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zurich_University "Zurich University") had already made a similar move. Drach-Temam criticised the rankings because the methodologies were not transparent and they could not be reproduced or questioned. She called them "black boxes" and noted they were run by commercial companies.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-norank-49)

# What are the world's best universities?

So vital is education to the future of society, billionaire Jack Ma has just stepped down from Alibaba to focus on it. But does it matter where you go to be educated?

The former teacher, who studied for a BA in English at Hangzhou Normal University, told the World Economic Forum he was [rejected from Harvard Business School 10 times](https://www.youtube.com/watch?time_continue=5&v=1O3ghiyirvU), but it didn't deter him from building a world-beating company.

Like Alibaba, universities in Ma's homeland China are starting to "expand their influence and presence on the world stage", according to the latest [Times Higher Eduction World University Rankings 2020](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2020/world-ranking).

Asia’s top two universities - Tsinghua (23rd) and Peking (24th) - are both in mainland China. With 81 institutions, China is also the fourth most-represented nation in the list for the fourth year in a row.

The US still dominates the list, with three of the top five and 172 institutions represented, compared with Japan’s 110 and the UK’s 100.

The THE says: "Overall, [China’s universities have improved](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/world-university-rankings-2020-reaching-critical-mass) in the areas of citation impact, share of international staff and share of international co-authorship over the past year, driven by higher levels of funding."

There are 11 more Iranian universities ranked this year, taking its total up to 40, and new regions whose institutions join the list for the first time this year include Brunei, Cuba, Malta, Montenegro, Puerto Rico and Vietnam.

[![](https://assets.weforum.org/editor/LFuiI1I1HgBoCTGFxHytEg9CKP34ixSmzPQt-fLZbVw.png?w=1024)](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-oxford)

Image: Times Higher Education

These are the top five:

**1. University of Oxford**

Topping the rankings for the fourth year in a row, Oxford prides itself on having an 'international character'. It's first overseas student, Emo of Friesland, was enrolled in 1190. Today, 40% of its faculty are from overseas.

[![](https://assets.weforum.org/editor/1FYoSXbC8EJTwX8_Fa8fDTopzBTLZ06ypNtAcmDeCUM.PNG?w=1024)](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-oxford)

Image: Times Higher Education

Among its famous alumni are 30 modern world leaders, including Bill Clinton, Indira Gandhi and the current British prime minister, Boris Johnson.

**2. California Institute of Technology**

Despite having an [unusual anti-growth model](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/world-university-rankings-2020-reaching-critical-mass), Caltech has risen three places to take the second spot this year, thanks to an improvement in its score for international staff.

[![](https://assets.weforum.org/editor/JiNFxKWZcR4YDjc7fZB9To1XHATr5hVDY570zFw4vOI.PNG?w=1024)](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-oxford)

Image: Times Higher Education

"We try to get better, not bigger," says its president, Thomas F. Rosenbaum.

Along with MIT, it's one of just two institutions in the ranking to achieve a score of more than 80 out of 100 in all five areas: teaching, research, citation impact, knowledge transfer and international outlook.

**3. University of Cambridge**

Like Oxford, Cambridge is a 'good all-rounder', but this year it slips from second to third place. It's called home by more than 18,000 students - including 4,000 international students from more than 120 countries.

[![](https://assets.weforum.org/editor/4DyIhvUNZryV1kN9IyRbqjk6FAhlfRWuTOE-NGq6fHY.PNG?w=1024)](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-oxford)

Image: Times Higher Education

It also boasts more than 100 libraries, which hold 15 million books.

**4. Stanford University**

Stanford has also dropped one place this year, to fourth.

Like the other two US institutions in the top 5, MIT and Caltech, is known for its technology focus.

[![](https://assets.weforum.org/editor/ra2C30LIjLoJv57hpHthXXmTvPKC4PjksDweYxrWNhI.PNG?w=1024)](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-oxford)

Image: Times Higher Education

THE says: "Companies founded by Stanford affiliates and alumni generate more than $2.7 trillion annual revenue - which would be the 10th largest economy in the world."

Among them are Google, Nike, Netflix, Hewlett-Packard and Instagram.

**5. Massachusetts Institute of Technology**

MIT rounds off the top five this year. Major scientific discoveries and advances accredited to the university include the development of radar, the first chemical synthesis of penicillin, the discovery of quarks, and the invention of magnetic core memory, which enabled the development of digital computers.

[![](https://assets.weforum.org/editor/Qa1vol0pvPBqmcSidIGMXCA0yzeiPJZVezGM5TP0bUs.PNG?w=1024)](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-oxford)

Image: Times Higher Education
